Judgment

1 By this judgment I will dispose of appeal u/sec.374 Cr.PC. filed on behalf of Rahisuddin @
Riyasuddin against the judgment dated 30.07.2015 and order on sentence dated 31.07.2015 passed by Sh. Gaurav Rao, then Ld. ACMM-II, Patiala House Court, New Delhi.
Rahisuddin @ Riyasuddin Vs. State 2

The brief facts of the case as per record and from trial court record are that accused is running an establishment namely M/s Janta Bakery at C-16/111,
Yamuna Vihar Road, North Ghonda, Delhi.

On 17.06.2004 at about 7.30 p.m. Food Inspector Sh. R.
K. Bhaskar visited the said place and purchased 600 grams of "Cream" from accused.
FI was accompanied with SDM/LHA Sh. S. C. Menz.
The said Cream was purchased for the purposes of analysis under PFA Act.
The same sample was divided into three parts, packed as per Rules of PFA.
Panchanama was prepared.
One sample was sent for analysis to Public Analyst.
As per the report of Analyst, sample did not confirm to the standard because "The sample does not conform to standard because milk fat is less than prescribed original limit of 60% (45.29%).
3 As the sample was failed, prosecution was launched by Food Inspector by filing complaint dated 25.10.2004 with the court.
Accused was summoned.
He has not exercised his right u/sec.13(2) PFA Act and get the sample analyzed by CFL.

Rahisuddin @ Riyasuddin vs The State on 10 November, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/3039309/
1 4

Charge was framed against accused u/sec.2(ia) (a) &
(m) read with sec.7 of PFA Act, 1954 punishable u/sec.16(1a) of PFA Act.

5 After trial, vide judgment dated 30.07.2015 accused was convicted for offence u/sec.16(1a) of PFA Act and vide order on sentence dated 31.07.2015 was directed to undergo simple  Rahisuddin @ Riyasuddin Vs. State imprisonment for a period of 8 months and fine of Rs.10,000/- and in default of payment of fine SI of 30 days.
6

In this appeal, the accused has assailed the judgment on the following grounds:-
(i) Non-compliance of Sec.10(7) of PFA Act and Rule i.e. independent witnesses were not joined.
(ii) Non-compliance of Rule 14 of PFA Rules i.e. the spoon, were not made clean and dried at the spot by the food inspector or any other official.
(iii) FI failed to inquiry as to what type of cream was that and due to that reason benefit be given to the appellant.
(iv) There was faulty sampling as the cream should have been taken with plunger and not spoon.
(v) There was non-compliance of Sec.13(2) PFA Act.

(vi) After coming into Food Safety & Standards Act, the punishment is to be granted under the said Act (argued orally).
7
No reply was filed by respondent/state and the matter was argued orally.
8 I have gone through the record, Trial Court record and have heard the submissions of Ld. counsel for appellant and Ld. SPP for State.
9 It is argued by counsel for appellant that no public witness was present in the proceedings nor efforts were made to join any public witnesses.
As far as this argument is concerned, the  Rahisuddin @ Riyasuddin Vs. State same argument was raised before the Ld. Trial Court.
The same was dealt by the trial court from para 17 to 23 of the judgment.

As far as opinion/finding of the trial court regarding this argument is concerned, I do not find any infirmity in those findings and the same are upheld and the arguments regarding this fact does not find any force and thus rejected.
10 It is further argued that compliance u/sec.14 PFA Rules was not proved on record by the prosecution.
It is stated that witnesses are deposing differently with respect to the cleanliness of spoon etc.
It is further stated that it was the duty of the prosecution to prove these facts.
These arguments were also addressed before the trial court.

The relevant part of the judgment dealing with Rahisuddin @ Riyasuddin vs The State on 10 November, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/3039309/

sentences.text: these arguments are from para 24 to 43 of the judgment.
I have gone through the record and submissions forwarded.
As far as these witnesses are concerned, they have specifically stated that as to how the Cream was taken.
The witnesses had deposed that the same was taken from open steel container with the help of clean and dry big spoon and after thoroughly mixing it and then put in clean and dry bottles.
So, there is no material on record which shows that the "implements" were unclean.
There is no discrepancy in the testimony of the witnesses regarding these facts.
So, I do not find force in the arguments of Ld. counsel for appellant that there is non- compliance of Rule 14 PFA Rules, 1955.
Hence, those arguments are rejected and the opinion given by trial court in this regard is Rahisuddin @ Riyasuddin Vs. State upheld.
11 It is further argued that FI failed to inquiry as to what type of cream was that and due to that reason benefit be given to the appellant.
As far as this argument is concerned, the same argument was raised before the Ld. Trial Court.
The same was dealt by the trial court from para 101 to 102 of the judgment.

As far as opinion/finding of the trial court regarding this argument is concerned, I do not find any infirmity in those findings and the same are upheld and the arguments regarding this fact does not find any force and thus rejected.
Moreover from the perusal of A. 11.02.02 note, it is clearly mentioned that "cream sold without any indication about milk fat content shall be treated as high fat cream".
From the perusal of the entire testimony, it appears that the same was taken from a container without any label declaration.
So, the article is to be treated as high fat cream.

12 It is further argued that there was faulty sampling as the cream should have been taken with plunger and not spoon and thus there was not property homogenization of the sample and due to that reason benefit be given to the appellant.
As far as this argument is concerned, the same argument was raised before the Ld. Trial Court.
The same was dealt by the trial court from para 45 to 52 of the judgment.

As far as opinion/finding of the trial court regarding this argument is concerned, I do not find any infirmity in those findings and the same are upheld and the arguments regarding this fact does Rahisuddin @ Riyasuddin Vs. State not find any force and thus rejected.
13 It is further argued that there was non-compliance of Sec.13(2) PFA Act and due to that reason benefit be given to the appellant.
As far as this argument is concerned, the same argument was raised before the Ld. Trial Court.
The same was dealt by the trial court from para 53 to 79 of the judgment.

As far as opinion/finding of the trial court regarding this argument is concerned, I do not find any infirmity in those findings and the same are upheld and the arguments regarding this fact does not find any force and thus rejected.
So, in these circumstances, I do not find any ground for change/modification of Trial Court's judgment, on merits.
So, the finding of the trial court with respect to the conviction of accused u/sec.2(ia) (a) & (m) of PFA Act 1954 read with Sec.16(1a) of PFA Act, is upheld.
14 It is submitted by Ld. counsel for appellant that on the date of judgment/order on sentence, the PFA Act, 1954 was repealed.
It is further stated that the court should have passed the order on sentence as per the quantum/punishment mentioned in Food and Safety Standards Act, 2006 (hereinafter called FSSA).

For this purpose, Ld. counsel for appellant had relied on Judgment i.e.
Rahisuddin @ Riyasuddin vs The State on 10 November, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/3039309/

sentences.text: On the other hand, it is argued by Ld. SPP for State that the sentencing cannot be done in new Act since the definition of many offences are changed in the new Act including this particular offence of which accused is charged.
Definition of major offences like "adulteration" and "misbranding" have been changed.

Now FSSA have definition "substandard food", "food containing extraneous matter",
"unsafe food" and "misbranded food".
Due to this reason, the ingredients have changed and thus there is no way in which the old offences could be related to new offences.

16 As far as the objection of Ld. SPP for State is concerned, in the present case, the offence was that the article/food i.e. Cream was found having slight deviations from standards i.e. milk fat on dry weight basis was found 45.29% (not less than 60%).
This was termed as adulteration in view of Sec.2(ia) of PFA Act and thus consequently punishable u/sec.16(1a) of PFA Act.
The charge was framed with these facts.
There was no charge in which it is stated that the said deviation was injurious to health.
Had it been the case, the charge should have been u/sec.16(1A) (ii) of PFA Act.
17 Now in the FSSA, such adulteration is termed as "substandard" in terms of Sec.3(zx) of FSSA Act punishable u/sec.51 of FSSA.
Rahisuddin @ Riyasuddin Vs.
State So, if we go through both these provisions of law, a particular offence with a particular fact is mentioned with some other name but with same ingredients in the new FSSA Act.
18 Hence, it is held that it is the ingredients which constitute an offence, determines that whether it is the same offence but with new name or an altogether different offence.

Here the offence i.e.
Cream having deviations from standards i.e. milk fat was found 45.29% (not less than 60%) which was punishable u/sec.16(1a) PFA Act is similar to the offence u/sec.51 of FSSA Act.
19 As far as the application of Nemi Chand judgment (supra) is concerned, the same is based on the old judgment i.e. T. Barai (supra) of Hon. Supreme Court.

The relevant portion of the T. Barai judgment is as follows:-
(Para 25) - It is settled both on authority and principle that when a later statute again describes an offence created by an earlier statute and imposes a different punishment, or varies the procedure, the earlier statute is repealed by implication.
In Michell v. Brown [(1958) 120 ER 909, 912: 32 LTOS 146 : 7 WR 80] Lord Campbell put the matter thus:

sentences.text:
In Regina v. Youle [(1861) 158 ER 311, 315-16: 4 LT 299: 9 WR 637] , Martin, B. said in the oft-quoted passage:
 Rahisuddin @ Riyasuddin Vs. State

"If a statute deals with a particular class of offences, and a subsequent Act is passed which deals with precisely the same offences, and a different punishment is imposed by the later Act, I think that, in effect, the legislature has declared that the new Act shall be substituted for the earlier Act."

The rule is however subject to the limitation contained in Article 20(1) against ex post facto law providing for a greater punishment and has also no application where the offence described in the later Act is not the same as in the earlier Act i.e. when the essential ingredients of the two offences are different.

Moreover this particular aspect is stated as a illustration in the same judgment in para 23 which is as follows:-
To illustrate, if Parliament were to reenact Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code,
1860 and provide that the punishment for an offence of murder shall be sentence for imprisonment for life instead of the present sentence of death or imprisonment for life
, then it cannot be that the courts would still award a sentence of death even in pending cases.
So, in these circumstances, it can be safely said that while considering on the point of sentence, the quantum of sentence in new Act i.e. FSSA is to be considered.

20 Now according to my aforesaid reasoning the offence i.e. Cream having deviations from standards i.e. milk fat on dry weight basis was found 45.29% (not less than 60%), earlier punishable u / s e c .
